steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the overview section of a Wikipedia article on 8.3 filenames: the basic naming rules and how VFAT, NTFS and other file systems handle short names alongside long filenames.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Basic 8.3 rules (length, extension, case)
- ## VFAT and computer-generated 8.3 filenames
  - VFAT long filenames
  - Auto-generated short names for backward compatibility
  - Windows naming convention, with examples
  - NTFS, ISO 9660, encoding, ReFS

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Basic rules
  - max eight characters (after directory specifier), optional extension: period . + at most three characters
  - systems supporting only 8.3: excess characters ignored
  - no extension: trailing . insignificant (myfile = myfile.)
  - names uppercase, though systems usually case-insensitive (CamelCap.tpu = CAMELCAP.TPU)
  - non-8.3 OSes (almost any modern OS) accessing 8.3 file systems (DOS floppies, some modern memory cards, networked file systems): may alter names internally to preserve case, avoid truncation, e.g. VFAT
- ## VFAT and computer-generated 8.3 filenames
- VFAT
  - FAT variant with extended directory format; Windows 95 and Windows NT 3.5
  - mixed-case Unicode long filenames (LFNs) plus classic 8.3 names
  - multiple 32-byte directory entry records per LFN; old 8.3 software recognizes only one as valid
- Generated names
  - backward compatibility with legacy apps (DOS, Windows 3.1) on FAT/VFAT: OS auto-generates 8.3 name for every LFN; file can [also] be opened, renamed, deleted through it
  - generated name (e.g. OVI3KV~N) may look little like original
  - NTFS: generation can be turned off system-wide (with risks)
  - Kernel32.dll function GetShortPathName returns 8.3 name
- Windows convention (no compulsory algorithm)
  - LFN 8.3 uppercase: no LFN stored. Example TEXTFILE.TXT
  - LFN 8.3 mixed case: LFN stores mixed-case name, 8.3 name uppercase. TextFile.Txt -> TEXTFILE.TXT
  - over 8 chars / invalid chars (space: disallowed by convention not APIs; those disallowed in directory tables) / extension over 3 chars: strip invalid chars; leading periods removed; + etc. -> underscore _; uppercase; truncate basename to first 6 chars + tilde + single digit + period . + first 3 chars of extension
    - TextFile.Mine.txt -> TEXTFI~1.TXT (or TEXTFI~2.TXT if ~1 exists); ver +1.2.text -> VER_12~1.TEX; .bashrc.swp -> BASHRC~1.SWP
  - all NT versions incl. Windows 2000+: at least 4 existing with same extension + first 6 chars -> first 2 chars of basename (1 if basename is 1 char) + 4 hex digits from undocumented hash + tilde + digit + period . + first 3 of extension. TextFile.Mine.txt -> TE021F~1.TXT
  - Windows 95, 98, ME: more than 9 collisions (~1 to ~9 not enough) -> truncate to 5 letters + tilde + two digits from 10 + period . + first 3 of extension. TEXTF~10.TXT if TEXTFI~1.TXT to TEXTFI~9.TXT exist
- MICROS~1 / MICROS~2: 2001 Microsoft antitrust case joke, companies after proposed split
- NTFS: Windows NT family, native LFNs, 8.3 names still for legacy apps; Windows NTVDM uses them; can disable system-wide for performance with many similarly named files in a folder; disable system-wide and/or per-volume; strip existing names via fsutil or Registry key
- ISO 9660 (mainly CDs): similar limits at Level 1, directory names no extensions, some chars (hyphens) not allowed; Level 2 up to 31 chars, more compatible with classic AmigaOS and classic Mac OS
- VFAT and NTFS store 8.3 names as ANSI encoding, backward compatibility
- ReFS no longer supports 8.3 filenames

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
8.3 filenames can have at most eight characters (after any directory specifier), and then optionally a filename extension that consists of a period . and at most three more characters. On systems that only support 8.3 filenames, the extra characters are ignored. If there is no extension, then a trailing . does not mean anything (so myfile and myfile. are the same). Also, file and directory names are uppercase in this system, even though systems that use the 8.3 standard are usually case-insensitive (so CamelCap.tpu is the same as the name CAMELCAP.TPU). But when non-8.3 operating systems (which is almost any modern operating system) access 8.3 file systems (such as DOS-formatted floppy disks, but also some modern memory cards and networked file systems), the underlying system may change the filenames internally so that case is kept and letters in the names are not truncated, for example in the case of VFAT.

### VFAT and computer-generated 8.3 filenames

VFAT is a variant of FAT that has an extended directory format, and it was introduced in Windows 95 and Windows NT 3.5. It allowed mixed-case Unicode long filenames (LFNs) as well as the classic 8.3 names. It did this by using multiple 32-byte directory entry records for long filenames (in a way that old 8.3 system software only recognizes one of them as the valid directory entry).

For backward-compatibility with legacy applications (on DOS and Windows 3.1), the operating system on FAT and VFAT filesystems automatically generates an 8.3 filename for every LFN, and the file can [also] be opened, renamed, or deleted through this name, although the name that is generated (e.g. OVI3KV~N) may not look much like the original. On NTFS filesystems the generation of 8.3 filenames can be turned off system-wide (with risks). You can get the 8.3 filename with the Kernel32.dll function GetShortPathName.

There is no compulsory algorithm for making the 8.3 name from an LFN, but Windows uses this convention:

If the LFN is 8.3 uppercase, then no LFN is stored on disk at all.

Example: TEXTFILE.TXT

If the LFN is 8.3 mixed case, the LFN stores the mixed-case name, and the 8.3 name is an uppercase version of it.

Example: TextFile.Txt becomes TEXTFILE.TXT.

- LFN over 8 chars / invalid chars (space: disallowed by convention not APIs; those disallowed in directory tables) / extension over 3 chars: strip invalid chars; remove leading periods; + etc. -> underscore _; uppercase; first 6 chars of basename + tilde + one digit + period . + first 3 chars of extension
  - TextFile.Mine.txt -> TEXTFI~1.TXT (or TEXTFI~2.TXT); ver +1.2.text -> VER_12~1.TEX; .bashrc.swp -> BASHRC~1.SWP
- all NT versions incl. Windows 2000 and later: at least 4 collisions -> first 2 chars of basename (or 1) + 4 hex digits from undocumented hash + tilde + digit + . + 3 chars of extension; TE021F~1.TXT
- Windows 95, 98, ME: more than 9 collisions -> 5 letters + tilde + two digits from 10; TEXTF~10.TXT
- MICROS~1 / MICROS~2, 2001 Microsoft antitrust case joke
- NTFS: native LFNs, 8.3 still for legacy apps, NTVDM; disable for performance; system-wide and/or per-volume; strip with fsutil or Registry key
- ISO 9660: Level 1 similar limits, no extensions on directory names, hyphens not allowed; Level 2 up to 31 chars (AmigaOS, Mac OS)
- VFAT/NTFS store 8.3 names as ANSI
- ReFS: no 8.3 support

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
8.3 filenames can have at most eight characters (after any directory specifier), and then optionally a filename extension that consists of a period . and at most three more characters. On systems that only support 8.3 filenames, the extra characters are ignored. If there is no extension, then a trailing . does not mean anything (so myfile and myfile. are the same). Also, file and directory names are uppercase in this system, even though systems that use the 8.3 standard are usually case-insensitive (so CamelCap.tpu is the same as the name CAMELCAP.TPU). But when non-8.3 operating systems (which is almost any modern operating system) access 8.3 file systems (such as DOS-formatted floppy disks, but also some modern memory cards and networked file systems), the underlying system may change the filenames internally so that case is kept and letters in the names are not truncated, for example in the case of VFAT.

### VFAT and computer-generated 8.3 filenames

VFAT is a variant of FAT that has an extended directory format, and it was introduced in Windows 95 and Windows NT 3.5. It allowed mixed-case Unicode long filenames (LFNs) as well as the classic 8.3 names. It did this by using multiple 32-byte directory entry records for long filenames (in a way that old 8.3 system software only recognizes one of them as the valid directory entry).

For backward-compatibility with legacy applications (on DOS and Windows 3.1), the operating system on FAT and VFAT filesystems automatically generates an 8.3 filename for every LFN, and the file can [also] be opened, renamed, or deleted through this name, although the name that is generated (e.g. OVI3KV~N) may not look much like the original. On NTFS filesystems the generation of 8.3 filenames can be turned off system-wide (with risks). You can get the 8.3 filename with the Kernel32.dll function GetShortPathName.

There is no compulsory algorithm for making the 8.3 name from an LFN, but Windows uses this convention:

If the LFN is 8.3 uppercase, then no LFN is stored on disk at all.

Example: TEXTFILE.TXT

If the LFN is 8.3 mixed case, the LFN stores the mixed-case name, and the 8.3 name is an uppercase version of it.

Example: TextFile.Txt becomes TEXTFILE.TXT.

If the LFN has more than 8 characters, or invalid characters such as space (which was disallowed by convention but not by the APIs) and the ones disallowed within directory tables, or an extension longer than 3 characters, then the invalid characters are stripped from the name. Leading periods . at the start of the name are removed. Other characters like + are changed to the underscore _, and the letters are made uppercase. Then the stripped name is truncated to the first 6 characters of its basename, and then comes a tilde, then a single digit, then a period ., then the first 3 characters of the extension.

Example: TextFile.Mine.txt becomes TEXTFI~1.TXT (or TEXTFI~2.TXT, if TEXTFI~1.TXT already exists). ver +1.2.text becomes VER_12~1.TEX. .bashrc.swp becomes BASHRC~1.SWP

On all NT versions, which includes Windows 2000 and later, if there are already at least 4 files or folders with the same extension and the same first 6 characters in their short names, the stripped LFN is truncated to the first 2 characters of the basename instead (or 1 if the basename only has 1 character), and then come 4 hexadecimal digits derived from an undocumented hash of the filename, then a tilde, then a single digit, then a period ., then the first 3 characters of the extension.

Example: TextFile.Mine.txt becomes TE021F~1.TXT.

On Windows 95, 98 and ME, if there are more than 9 files or folders with the same extension and first 6 characters in their short names (so the ~1 through ~9 suffixes are not enough to resolve the collision), the name is truncated more, to 5 letters, then a tilde, then two digits starting from 10, then a period . and the first 3 characters of the extension.

Example: TextFile.Mine.txt becomes TEXTF~10.TXT if TEXTFI~1.TXT through TEXTFI~9.TXT all already exist.

In the 2001 Microsoft antitrust case, people used the names MICROS~1 and MICROS~2 as a joke for the companies that might exist after a proposed split of Microsoft.

NTFS is a file system used by the Windows NT family. It supports LFNs natively, but 8.3 names are still available for legacy applications. Windows NTVDM is known to use 8.3 names. This can be disabled system-wide if wanted, to improve performance when there are large numbers of similarly named files in the same folder. The creation of 8.3 filenames can be disabled system-wide and/or per-volume, and existing 8.3 filenames can be stripped with fsutil or a Registry key.

The ISO 9660 file system (which is mainly used on compact discs) has similar limitations at the most basic Level 1, and in addition directory names cannot have extensions and some characters (notably hyphens) are not allowed in filenames. Level 2 allows filenames up to 31 characters, which is more compatible with classic AmigaOS and classic Mac OS filenames.

On VFAT and NTFS file systems, 8.3 filenames are stored as ANSI encoding, for backward-compatibility.

ReFS does not support 8.3 filenames anymore.

steps.text:
8.3 filenames are limited to at most eight characters (after any directory specifier), optionally followed by a filename extension consisting of a period . and at most three further characters. On systems that only support 8.3 filenames, excess characters are ignored. If a file name has no extension, a trailing . has no significance (that is, myfile and myfile. are equivalent). Furthermore, file and directory names are uppercase in this system, even though systems that use the 8.3 standard are usually case-insensitive (making CamelCap.tpu equivalent to the name CAMELCAP.TPU). However, on non-8.3 operating systems (such as almost any modern operating system) that access 8.3 file systems (including DOS-formatted floppy disks, but also some modern memory cards and networked file systems), the underlying system may alter filenames internally to preserve case and to avoid truncating letters in the names, for example in the case of VFAT.

### VFAT and computer-generated 8.3 filenames

VFAT, a variant of FAT with an extended directory format, was introduced in Windows 95 and Windows NT 3.5. It allowed mixed-case Unicode long filenames (LFNs) in addition to classic 8.3 names, by using multiple 32-byte directory entry records for long filenames (in such a way that old 8.3 system software will only recognize one of them as the valid directory entry).

To maintain backward-compatibility with legacy applications (on DOS and Windows 3.1), on FAT and VFAT filesystems the operating system automatically generates an 8.3 filename for every LFN, through which the file can [also] be opened, renamed, or deleted, although the generated name (e.g. OVI3KV~N) may show little similarity to the original. On NTFS filesystems the generation of 8.3 filenames can be turned off system-wide (with risks).[1] The 8.3 filename can be obtained using the Kernel32.dll function GetShortPathName.[2,3]

While there is no compulsory algorithm for creating the 8.3 name from an LFN, Windows uses the following convention:[4]

If the LFN is 8.3 uppercase, no LFN will be stored on disk at all.

Example: TEXTFILE.TXT

If the LFN is 8.3 mixed case, the LFN will store the mixed-case name, while the 8.3 name will be an uppercase version of it.

Example: TextFile.Txt becomes TEXTFILE.TXT.

If the LFN contains more than 8 characters, invalid characters such as space (which was disallowed by convention though not by the APIs) and those disallowed within directory tables, or an extension longer than 3 characters, the name is stripped of its invalid characters. If the name begins with periods . the leading periods are removed. Other characters such as + are changed to the underscore _, and letters are put in uppercase. The stripped name is then truncated to the first 6 characters of its basename, followed by a tilde, a single digit, a period ., and the first 3 characters of the extension.

Example: TextFile.Mine.txt becomes TEXTFI~1.TXT (or TEXTFI~2.TXT, should TEXTFI~1.TXT already exist). ver +1.2.text becomes VER_12~1.TEX. .bashrc.swp becomes BASHRC~1.SWP

On all NT versions, including Windows 2000 and later, if at least 4 files or folders already exist with the same extension and first 6 characters in their short names, the stripped LFN is instead truncated to the first 2 characters of the basename (or 1 if the basename has only 1 character), followed by 4 hexadecimal digits derived from an undocumented hash of the filename, a tilde, a single digit, a period ., and the first 3 characters of the extension.[5]

Example: TextFile.Mine.txt becomes TE021F~1.TXT.

On Windows 95, 98 and ME, if there are more than 9 files or folders with the same extension and first 6 characters in their short names (so that the ~1 through ~9 suffixes aren't enough to resolve the collision), the name is further truncated to 5 letters, followed by a tilde, two digits starting from 10, a period . and the first 3 characters of the extension.

Example: TextFile.Mine.txt becomes TEXTF~10.TXT if TEXTFI~1.TXT through TEXTFI~9.TXT all exist already.

During the 2001 Microsoft antitrust case, the names MICROS~1 and MICROS~2 were humorously used to refer to the companies that might exist after a proposed split of Microsoft.[6]

NTFS, a file system used by the Windows NT family, supports LFNs natively, but 8.3 names are still available for legacy applications; Windows NTVDM is known to use them. This can optionally be disabled system-wide to improve performance in situations where large numbers of similarly named files exist in the same folder.[1] 8.3 filename creation can be disabled system-wide and/or per-volume, and existing 8.3 filenames can be stripped using fsutil or a Registry key.[7]

The ISO 9660 file system (mainly used on compact discs) has similar limitations at the most basic Level 1, with the additional restriction that directory names cannot contain extensions and that some characters (notably hyphens) are not allowed in filenames. Level 2 allows filenames of up to 31 characters, which is more compatible with classic AmigaOS and classic Mac OS filenames.

On VFAT and NTFS file systems, 8.3 filenames are stored as ANSI encoding, for backward-compatibility.

ReFS no longer supports 8.3 filenames.
